title: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers
goal: By the end you can explain what `A.() -> B` is on the JVM, write a nested builder DSL with validation, use `@DslMarker` so misplaced calls stop compiling, and give Java callers a way in.

warmup.q: Inside `payer { }` of a payment-request DSL with no `@DslMarker`, someone writes `payee { name = "oops" }` by mistake. What happens?
options: It doesn't compile: `payee` isn't a member of `PartyBuilder`
It compiles and calls `payee` on the outer `PaymentRequestBuilder`
It compiles and builds a payee nested inside the payer
It compiles and is ignored at run time
warmup.why: Both receivers are in scope inside `payer { }`, and Kotlin resolves an unqualified call against each of them, nearest first. `PartyBuilder` has no `payee`, so the outer builder's `payee` is used. `@DslMarker` exists to turn that into a compile error. The first option is what most people expect, which is exactly why the bug survives review.

sections.h: Calling a DSL from Java, and what became of context receivers
sections.body:
A Kotlin DSL works from Java, though it isn't pretty. Every `Builder.() -> Unit` parameter is a `Function1<Builder, Unit>`, so the Java caller writes `b -> { b.debit(...); return Unit.INSTANCE; }`, and the lab's `LedgerFromJavaTest` does just that. If Java callers matter, add a thin overload that takes a `java.util.function.Consumer` and give it its own name, so Kotlin callers never have to choose between two lambda types:

```java
JournalEntry e = LedgerKt.journalEntryJava("payout-981", b -> {
    b.debit("merchant:981", 12_000L);
    b.credit("bank:clearing", 12_000L);      // a void lambda: no Unit.INSTANCE
});
```

```kotlin
fun journalEntryJava(id: String, block: Consumer<EntryBuilder>): JournalEntry =
    journalEntry(id) { block.accept(this) }   // `this` is the EntryBuilder
```

`@DslMarker` means nothing to Java. A Java lambda names its parameter, so the scope problem doesn't arise.

DSLs were also the main reason for an experiment you'll still find in older code and blog posts: context receivers. Kotlin 1.6.20 shipped them as a prototype behind `-Xcontext-receivers`, and its release notes warned that the compiler would "produce pre-release binaries that cannot be used in production code". They let a function demand a receiver from its surroundings, as in `context(Logger) fun audit()`, so a DSL function could require being called inside some scope. Kotlin 2.2.0 replaced them with context parameters, and the 2.3.20 notes say it plainly: "Experimental context receivers are no longer supported and are replaced by context parameters."

In Kotlin 2.4.21 the old syntax fails twice: `context parameters must be named. Use '_' to declare an anonymous context parameter.` and then `unresolved reference 'log'`, because a context parameter is not a receiver in the body. The old flag fails too: `experimental context receivers are superseded by context parameters. Remove the '-Xcontext-receivers' compiler argument and migrate to the new syntax.` When you see either message, the fix is the next lesson: context parameters, stable since Kotlin 2.4.0.

A check before you move on: a Java caller passes `b -> { b.debit("merchant:981", 100L); b.credit("bank:clearing", 100L); }` to `journalEntry`, with no `return` at the end. Predict what javac says, and why the same lambda is fine for `journalEntryJava`. (The answer follows from the two interfaces: `Function1.invoke` returns a value, and `Consumer.accept` returns `void`.)

analogy: A lambda with receiver is like being handed a form already clipped to a clipboard: inside the block you write on that form without saying which one. Nested blocks stack forms on top of each other, and without `@DslMarker` a field that doesn't exist on the top form gets written onto the form underneath, without anyone noticing. The marker says only the top form may be written on without naming it. The analogy breaks in a good way: a clerk finds the misfiled field after the forms are sent, while the compiler finds it before the code ever runs.
in_your_world: Payment services build nested data all day: a payout batch with entries and postings, routing rules per merchant, a test fixture for a Kafka event with its headers. A small DSL makes Quarkus tests and fixtures read like the data they produce, and it puts the validation (debits equal credits, every party has an IBAN) in one `build()` instead of in every test. Keep DSLs for nested data that many people write; a flat request with six fields is clearer with named arguments. Put `@DslMarker` in from the first day. Adding it later breaks every call site that was quietly reaching an outer builder, which is the point, but finding them in a hundred tests is a bad afternoon.

compare.title: A journal-entry builder: Java Consumer vs Kotlin lambda with receiver

java.title: Journal.java

kotlin.title: Journal.kt
kotlin.src:
fun journalEntry(id: String, block: EntryBuilder.() -> Unit): JournalEntry =
    EntryBuilder(id).apply(block).build()   // the builder is `this` inside block

val e = journalEntry("payout-981") {
    memo = "merchant payout"
    debit("merchant:981", 12_000)
    credit("bank:clearing", 11_850)
    credit("revenue:fees", 150)
}

compare.note: Both compile to the same thing: a function object that receives the builder. On the JVM, Kotlin's `EntryBuilder.() -> Unit` is a `Function1<EntryBuilder, Unit>`, and Java's `Consumer<EntryBuilder>` plays the same role. The difference is only in the source: Kotlin makes the builder `this`, so the block reads like a list of statements, and nested blocks need `@DslMarker` to stop calls from reaching outer builders by accident. Java names the parameter every time, which is noisier but can never resolve a call against the wrong builder.

worked.title: Add vocabulary to the ledger DSL with an extension function

steps.say: Every merchant payout is the same three postings: debit the merchant's balance, credit the bank with the net amount, credit fee revenue. Written out each time, the arithmetic gets copied, and one day it's copied wrong.
Write an extension function on the builder. It works even if `EntryBuilder` lives in a library you can't edit, and inside a block it reads like a built-in word.

Check where it can be called. Inside `entry { }` it resolves against the nearest receiver, the `EntryBuilder`. Inside `batch { }` but outside an entry, it doesn't compile, so a payout can't be posted outside an entry by accident.

Run it: the entry has postings of 12,000 debit, 11,850 and 150 credit, and `build()` accepts it because the debits equal the credits. Integer division rounds the fee down, so the bank gets the extra cent. Whether that's right is a business rule, and it's now in one function you can test.

lab.title: A double-entry journal DSL
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail.
In `EntryBuilder`, keep the postings in a private list, and write `debit` and `credit` so they reject an amount of 0 or less (TODO 1).
Write `build()` (TODO 2): at least two postings, debits equal to credits, and a copy of the list in the result.
Write `BatchBuilder` (TODO 3) and the two entry functions (TODO 4). Each is one or two lines once `EntryBuilder` works.
Before adding the marker, write a scratch function with `entry("e2") { ... }` inside another `entry { }`. It compiles. Then put `@LedgerDsl` on both builders (TODO 5) and read the error.
Run until all seven pass, including `LedgerFromJavaTest`, which builds an entry from Java with a `Function1`.
hints: A private helper `post(account, side, amountMinor)` that calls `require(amountMinor > 0) { ... }` and then `postings += Posting(...)` keeps `debit` and `credit` to one line each.
`postings.filter { it.side == Side.DEBIT }.sumOf { it.amountMinor }` gives the debit total.
`postings.toList()` makes the copy, so later calls on the builder can't change an entry you already built.
In `BatchBuilder.entry`, the parameter `id` shadows the property. Use `this.id` for the batch id in the error message.

recap: `A.() -> B` is a function type with receiver: inside the lambda, the `A` is `this`. On the JVM it's a `Function1<A, B>`, interchangeable with `(A) -> B`.
A DSL is builder classes plus entry functions of the form `Builder().apply(block).build()`. No library is needed.
`buildList`, `buildMap` and `buildString` give you a mutable receiver while building and a read-only result.
Validate single values at the call, and cross-field rules in `build()`.
`@DslMarker` on the builder classes makes only the nearest receiver implicit; reach outer ones with `this@label`. On functions it does nothing.
Java calls a DSL with `Function1` lambdas that `return Unit.INSTANCE`. Context receivers are gone since 2.3.20; context parameters replace them.

quiz.q: What is the JVM type of a parameter declared as `block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit`?
options: `kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<Unit>`
`kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<PartyBuilder, Unit>`
`java.util.function.Consumer<PartyBuilder>`
A generated interface named `PartyBuilderBlock`
quiz.why: The receiver becomes the first parameter, so a receiver lambda with no other parameters is a `Function1`. That's why Java passes `p -> { ...; return Unit.INSTANCE; }`. `Consumer` is Java's idiom for the same job, not what Kotlin compiles to.

quiz.q: Both builders carry `@PaymentDsl`. Which of these compiles inside `payer { }`?
options: `payee { name = "x" }`
`currency = "GBP"`
`this@paymentRequest.currency = "GBP"`
None of them
quiz.why: With the marker, members of the outer `PaymentRequestBuilder` can't be reached implicitly, so `payee { }` and `currency = ...` are errors. An explicit label names the outer receiver on purpose, and that is allowed.

quiz.q: You put `@PaymentDsl` on the functions `payer`, `payee` and `paymentRequest`, but not on the builder classes. What happens to `payee { }` written inside `payer { }`?
options: It compiles and calls the outer builder's `payee`: a marker on functions has no effect
A compile error: implicit receiver not allowed
It always throws at run time
A compiler warning, then it runs
quiz.why: The docs say a DSL marker counts only on classes, receiver types in function types and type aliases. On functions or properties it has no effect, so the scope check never starts and the misplaced call resolves against the outer builder.

quiz.q: What does `buildList { add(1); if (size == 1) add(2) }` return, and can you add to it afterwards?
options: `[1, 2]`, and casting it to `MutableList` lets you add
`[1]`, because `size` was read before `add`
It doesn't compile: `size` isn't available inside the block
`[1, 2]`, and it's read-only: `add` after a cast throws `UnsupportedOperationException`
quiz.why: Inside the block `this` is a `MutableList`, so `size` is 1 after the first `add` and the second element is added. The returned list is read-only even if you cast it, which is the point of a builder: mutable while building, fixed afterwards.

quiz.q: From the patterns track: a `ChargeRequest` has six flat fields and no nested parts. What's the best way to build it in Kotlin?
options: A type-safe DSL with `@DslMarker`
A constructor with named and default arguments
A Java-style builder with setters and `build()`
A `buildMap` of field names to values
quiz.why: Named and default arguments already give readable, checked construction for flat data. A DSL earns its two extra classes only when the data nests, like items under a request or postings under an entry.

flashcards.back: A function type with receiver: inside the lambda, the `A` is `this`. On the JVM it's `Function1<A, B>`.
Yes. The receiver is just the first parameter: you can assign one to the other and call either as `f(sb)`.

flashcards.front: What does `@DslMarker` change inside a nested block?
flashcards.back: Only the nearest receiver marked with that annotation is implicit. Outer marked receivers need an explicit `this@label`.

flashcards.front: Where must a DSL marker annotation go to have any effect?
flashcards.back: On the builder classes (or a common superclass), on receiver types of function types, or on type aliases. On functions or properties it does nothing.
A `MutableList` as `this` while you build, and a read-only `List` as the result. It's inline, so the lambda costs nothing.

flashcards.front: How does Java call `fun journalEntry(id: String, block: EntryBuilder.() -> Unit)`?
flashcards.back: With a `Function1<EntryBuilder, Unit>`: `b -> { b.debit(...); return Unit.INSTANCE; }`.
A 1.6.20 prototype behind `-Xcontext-receivers`, replaced by context parameters in 2.2.0, and no longer supported since 2.3.20.

terms.plain: A lambda in which one object is `this`, so its members can be called without a prefix.
A type such as `A.() -> B`. On the JVM, the receiver is the first parameter of a `Function1`.
Builder classes plus functions that take receiver lambdas, so nested data can be written as code the compiler checks.
Meta-annotation for an annotation that marks DSL receivers. Inside a block, only the nearest marked receiver is implicit.
An object whose members you can call without naming it, such as `this` inside a receiver lambda.
`this@paymentRequest`: names an outer receiver by the function that introduced it.
An experimental feature (1.6.20) that let a function require a receiver from its scope. Replaced by context parameters.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's test builds a payment request with `payee { }` accidentally written inside `payer { }`, and it compiled. Explain why it compiled, and what `@DslMarker` changes.
explain_back.answer: Inside `payer { }` there are two implicit receivers: the `PartyBuilder` the block was given, and the outer `PaymentRequestBuilder` from the `paymentRequest { }` block around it. When Kotlin sees an unqualified call, it tries each receiver in scope, nearest first. `PartyBuilder` has no `payee`, so the compiler found `payee` on the outer builder and called that, which built a second party in the wrong place. Nothing in the types was wrong, so it compiled. `@DslMarker` is a rule about those receivers: if the builder classes carry the same marker annotation, only the nearest marked receiver is implicit inside a block. The misplaced `payee { }` becomes a compile error that says it can't be called with an implicit receiver. If you really mean the outer builder, you name it with `this@paymentRequest`, which nobody writes by accident. The marker has to be on the builder classes; putting it on the functions does nothing.
